10052-the-open-door-and-the-portrait-sto:
Margaret Oliphant's 1881 stories of the seen and unseen open with The Open Door, in which a narrator takes the house of Brentwood on his return from India. The house suits his family and lies within reach of Edinburgh, where his boy Roland, whose schooling was neglected, can go in and out to school.

The second story, The Portrait, continues Oliphant's quiet supernatural manner, where the unseen presses gently on daily life. Oliphant writes without shock, letting mystery grow from a house, a picture, and a family. Readers get Victorian ghost stories of a thoughtful, humane kind.
10648-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-13:
John Lord's Beacon Lights of History closes with this thirteenth volume on great writers, finishing a plan he left incomplete at his death. It holds the lectures he had finished on leading men of letters, and adds essays by Emerson, Macaulay, Hedge, and Mercer Adam to fill the gaps. The publishers note that only work Lord himself had judged worthy was kept.

The lectures treat writers as forces in history, shaping thought and morals as surely as statesmen shape nations. Lord's warm, story-driven style carries through the volume. Readers get a final installment of a popular nineteenth-century series, and a view of which authors an earlier age counted as great.
13353-four-psalms-xxiii-xxxvi-lii-cxxi-i:
George Adam Smith interprets four psalms for everyday use in this small volume of the Little Books on Religion series. Psalm 23, Psalm 36, Psalm 52, and Psalm 121 are read not as ancient poems alone, but as words for people facing sin, danger, and the pull of comfort.

Smith pictures sinners as guests of God, welcomed whatever their past, and Christ standing between a person and what he flees. He warns the comfortable middle classes, who face a dozen small distractions each day that drown conscience. The readings are pastoral and plain, meant to turn familiar psalms into counsel for work, wealth, and daily conduct.
15436-journal-of-a-voyage-from-okkak-on-:
Benjamin Kohlmeister and George Kmoch, missionaries of the United Brethren, wrote this journal of a voyage from Okkak on the Labrador coast to Ungava Bay, west of Cape Chudleigh. Printed in London in 1814 for the Brethren's Society for the Furtherance of the Gospel, it aimed to explore the coast and visit the Esquimaux in that unknown region. A map in the HTML version marks the route.

The journal records coast, weather, meetings, and mission work in a remote Arctic shore, in the plain style of men reporting to supporters at home. Readers meet Inuit communities, traders, and fellow missionaries, and see how the Brethren planned new stations. As an early record of Labrador and Ungava, it preserves names, places, and encounters that later histories often pass over in silence.
16767-half-hours-with-the-telescope-bein:
Richard A. Proctor wrote this 1873 popular guide to the telescope, issued by Putnam's Sons in New York and printed in London. It teaches how to use a small telescope for fun and learning, what a good three-inch glass can show, how star maps work, and how telescopes are built. Plates on stone and wood show the sky and the tools.

Proctor writes for the new owner of a small glass, not for a trained star watcher. He points out which sights repay a look, how to find them, and what to expect at the eye piece. The book still charms as a first guide to night sky watching, and as a record of what home stargazing looked like in the 1870s.
20451-the-confessions-of-artemas-quibble:
Arthur Train, a lawyer who wrote comic fiction, edited The Confessions of Artemas Quibble as the mock memoir of a shady attorney. Quibble tells his own life story with pride. The joke is that he sees nothing wrong in it.

Quibble recalls a poor childhood after his mother's marriage. A parent's odd ways left the family with little money. The boy had to wear his stepfather's worn-out clerical clothes, which may explain his later dislike of all things churchly. From that start, the confessions follow a career of tricks played on clients, courts, and the law itself.
25588-outline-of-the-development-of-the-:
T. W. Van Metre writes this outline of the internal commerce of the United States from 1789 to 1900. It served as a thesis for a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania. Williams and Wilkins published it in Baltimore in 1913. It abstracts a longer work to come.

Van Metre defines internal commerce broadly as all trade in goods among people inside the Union after 1789. Roads, canals, railways, rivers, and markets trace how goods moved. Prices formed, and regions joined into one trading nation across the nineteenth century. The paper calls itself a brief abstract, promising a fuller work later.
29942-a-letter-to-hon-charles-sumner-wit:
Rev. H. W. Pierson, formerly president of Cumberland College, Kentucky, addressed this letter to Hon. Charles Sumner, printed in Washington in 1870. Its full title joins statements of outrages upon freedmen in Georgia with an account of Pierson's expulsion from Andersonville, Georgia, by the Ku-Klux Klan. Pierson was also the author of a life of Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and a corresponding member of the New York Historical Society.

A front letter from November 1861 shows George Bancroft, Hamilton Fish, William M. Evarts, and other signers urging Pierson to repeat his Jefferson paper before the Historical Society and to lecture more widely. The body of the pamphlet turns to lawlessness in Georgia, with statements of outrages and Pierson's own expulsion. The pamphlet is a primary document of Reconstruction violence, written by a witness and addressed to a senator.
4496-the-gentleman-of-fifty-and-the-dams:
George Meredith left this piece as an early, unfinished fragment, and it reads as the opening movement of a novel rather than a finished story. A narrator walks a narrow valley river, meets a vicar and his wife bathing in odd, comic circumstances, and begins to watch an older gentleman and a girl of nineteen. Age, rank, and attraction are set against each other from the first pages.

Because the fragment breaks off, readers get suggestion rather than resolution: witty talk, social observation, and a courtship that never reaches its end. Meredith's interest lies in how a man of fifty sees himself beside youth, and how a young woman judges him. It suits readers curious about a famous novelist's work in progress, and about Victorian ideas of age and marriage.
4762-civil-government-of-virginia-a-text:
Wm. F. Fox, superintendent of schools at Richmond, Virginia, wrote Civil Government of Virginia as a textbook for schools. It rests on the constitution of 1902, and conforms to laws enacted in accordance with it. Fox notes that important changes in every part of the state's fundamental law came from the constitutional convention of 1901 to 1902.

Many changes did not take full effect until as late as February 1, 1904, and some still awaited laws already passed or to be enacted. Fox trusts readers will pardon errors or omissions, while believing the work stands in harmony with constitution and laws as they stand. Contents cover general principles, bill of rights, voting and office holding, elections, the legislative department, and the executive department. Readers get a clear early twentieth-century civics textbook for Virginia schools.
8684-the-conquest-of-america-a-romance-o:
Cleveland Moffett imagined, in 1916, a German conquest of the United States in 1921, told through extracts from the diary of James E. Langston, war correspondent of the London Times. The frontispiece pictures German soldiers marching up Broadway on May 25, 1921, the day of capitulation, and halting outside the banking house of J. P. Morgan and Company. The frame gives the invasion the feel of reported fact.

Disaster chapters give way to a story of American recovery and victory, as the romance's subtitle promises. Moffett, author of Through the Wall and Careers of Danger and Daring, wrote invasion fiction at a moment when the Great War made such fears feel plausible. The novel now reads as a period warning tale, useful for students of propaganda and popular fear, and still brisk as an adventure of occupation and resistance.
9267-chip-of-the-flying-u:
B. M. Bower wrote this western ranch novel about Chip, of the Flying U ranch in Montana. The weekly mail arrives, Shorty makes his rounds, and the Old Man's sister sets the plot in motion. Chapters cross the Hog's Back, tend Silver in his stall, and hum with round-up preparation. Love and a stomach pump share a chapter title.

Chip's tale mixes humor, romance, and ranch work, with art critics, convalescence, and spoils of victory along the way. Charles Russell's illustrations grace the book. It remains a beloved western, brisk, funny, and true to cowboy life.
civil-government-of-virginia-a-text-book:
William Fayette Fox wrote Civil Government of Virginia as a text-book for schools. Fox, superintendent of schools in Richmond, based it on the constitution of 1902. His note warns that the convention of 1901-2 changed the state's fundamental law deeply. Some changes took full effect only in February 1904.

General principles, the bill of rights, voting, and elections come first. The legislative department follows, with the Senate, House of Delegates, and General Assembly. Executive chapters work through the governor down to the commissioners of the sinking fund. Courts receive two chapters, from the Supreme Court of Appeals to justices' courts. County, district, and city government complete the scheme. Fox aimed at accuracy a schoolboy could use, explaining every office a Virginian might meet or hold.

govdocs-archive_org-NewZealandUFO_Declas:
File AIR 39/3/3 is the New Zealand Defence Force's file on unidentified flying objects, opened in 1952 and closed in 1955 in its first volumes. The file, titled Flying Saucers in the usage of the day, was declassified in September 2010. Volumes one and two are preserved here.

Reports from pilots, servicemen, and the public, with official correspondence and press clippings, fill the file in the order the Air Force kept them. New Zealand's small official saucer archive mirrors those of larger powers: curiosity, caution, and no conclusions. The release made it the southern hemisphere's counterpart to the better-known British and American UFO files.
govdocs-archive_org-mkchickwit-mksearch-:
In 1977 the CIA's mind-control programs broke into the open, and newspapers covered the revelations day by day. This file compiles OCR'd press clippings from that year on three MKULTRA subprojects: MKCHICKWIT, MKSEARCH, and MKOFTEN.

The clippings include New York Times reporting on CIA-funded research at Georgetown University, money that reached the university through the Geschickter Foundation. Read in sequence, the stories show the scandal unfolding in public: secret funding, unwitting research subjects, and a university caught in the middle. The compilation preserves the mind-control story as the press told it at the time.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ExtremistsFBIUs: An FBI routing slip circulated among senior Bureau officials, including Clyde Tolson, J. Edgar Hoover's closest aide, and Mark Felt. A routing slip is the cover sheet that moves a paper from desk to desk inside the Bureau. The slip's substantive content cannot be recovered from the surviving fragment, so the record documents the circulation itself rather than any decision.
journal-of-a-voyage-from-okkak-on-the-co:
Benjamin Kohlmeister and George Kmoch's Journal of a Voyage tells of a mission journey along the Labrador coast. Both men were missionaries of the United Brethren, the Moravian Church. They sailed from Okkak toward Ungava Bay, west of Cape Chudleigh. Their aim was to explore the coast and visit the Esquimaux of that unknown region.

The London edition of 1814 was printed for the Brethren's Society for the Furtherance of the Gospel. That society spread the Moravian message among peoples its members called heathen. The journal records coasts, weather, and meetings with Inuit communities new to European missionaries. It stands as an early firsthand account of Labrador's far north and its people.
nasa-tm-19660007948-a-solution-for-satel:
Goddard's Dynamics and Advanced Missions group solved a neat orbital problem in this 1965 report, number DR 105. A satellite passes through shadow in each orbit. In full shadow, called umbra, it gets no sunlight at all. In partial shadow, or penumbra, it gets some. The report gives a way to compute the time spent in each state.

Shadow time decides power and heating for a satellite. Solar cells rest while batteries carry the load in darkness. The method is applied to a lunar satellite mission analysis. Mission planners could then size batteries and plan work with the shadow periods already known, rather than guessed.
nasa-tm-19660020395-feasibility-studies-:
Henry C Haller and Seymour Lieblein at Lewis Research Center studied radiators that shed a spacecraft's waste heat, in a paper for a June 1966 heat pipe meeting in New Mexico. Their design uses vapor chamber fins. A vapor chamber spreads heat evenly across a fin, so the whole fin glows with waste heat into space. The target use was Rankine cycle power plants for space.

A power plant in orbit has no air or water to carry heat away. Radiation from a hot surface is the only exit. Feasibility studies test whether a design can work at the needed size and weight. Haller and Lieblein give that test for a fin design that later space power work kept returning to.
nasa-tm-19680025171-oxygen-reclamation-f:
Joseph Weissbart, Wilson Smart, and Theodore Wydeven of Ames Research Center report oxygen reclamation from carbon dioxide in this paper. Long space missions need to recover oxygen from the carbon dioxide crews exhale. One promising method electrolyzes carbon dioxide at high temperature through a solid oxide electrolyte.

Only oxide ions can cross the solid electrolyte in an electric field. That property cleanly separates oxygen from the carbon dioxide stream. The paper reports a long-duration test of a small electrolyzer cell. Test tables track cell voltage, resistance, temperature, and gas flow over the run. Small amounts of water vapor in the feed gas acted as a catalyst for the cathode reaction.
nasa-tm-19720003678-a-thermosphere-compo:
Hasso B Niemann, Nelson W Spencer, and Gerald A Schmitt of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in July 1971, numbered X-621-71-300. It reports a measurement of atomic oxygen high in the atmosphere. Their instrument was a quadrupole mass spectrometer with a special ion source. It flew in the Thermosphere Probe. The side energy focusing design sharpened what the instrument could measure.

The team measured atomic oxygen between one hundred thirty and two hundred forty kilometers up. The ion source design raised the oxygen share among measured particles. That boost made the faint oxygen signal easier to read accurately. Atomic oxygen eats at spacecraft surfaces in low orbit. Knowing its amount by height helps predict satellite drag and decay.
podcast-joerogan-JtbGgSwuE_U:
Canadian politician Pierre Poilievre joins Joe Rogan for episode 2470. Poilievre leads Canada's Conservatives with a sharp, populist style. His plain talk on costs won him a huge base.

Rogan asks how Canada reached its current strain on housing and pay. Poilievre blames big government and pledges common sense. The talk crosses the border with ease, since both nations share gripes. The episode gives American listeners a northern leader in full. It suits the political and the curious about a neighbor in flux. Plain speech is his weapon and his brand.
the-conquest-of-america-a-romance-of-dis: Cleveland Moffett's 1916 novel imagines a German conquest of the United States in 1921, told through extracts from the diary of James E. Langston, a London Times war correspondent. A caption under the front picture describes German troops marching up Broadway on May 25, 1921, the day of surrender, and halting outside the banking house of J. P. Morgan and Company. Verses from Jeremiah and the Psalms stand at the front. Only the title pages, picture caption, verses, and the head of the contents are present here.
the-gentleman-of-fifty-and-the-damsel-of:
George Meredith left The Gentleman of Fifty and the Damsel of Nineteen as an early fragment, never finished. A narrator tells the tale as he walks by a river near Ickleworth Bridge.

Rounding a bend, the narrator finds bathers in the bright water below the vicar's terrace steps. To his shock the bathers are the vicar himself and his portly wife, both in full dress, standing waist deep and chatting as calmly as at tea. The vicar recites Greek verse to the sun while his wife fights her ballooning skirts. Meredith turns a droll scene into a study of an absent-minded scholar and the young watcher's own sly heart.
the-open-door-and-the-portrait-stories-o:
Margaret O. Wilson Oliphant published The Open Door, and The Portrait, Stories of the Seen and the Unseen, in 1881. The Open Door begins with a father who took the house of Brentwood, near Edinburgh, on his return from India. His only surviving son Roland, whose schooling had been neglected, rides to the High School each morning on his pony.

The doctor's plan lets the boy stay home yet attend school, and the northern air soon browns his pale face. Brentwood stands on a fine, wealthy slope of country. A sister record carries the same opening text word for word. Oliphant grounds her tale of the unseen in this settled family scene.
